title: Alkanes: naming and conformations
note: Name an alkane from its longest chain, number from the end nearer the first branch, and list substituents alphabetically. Staggered conformations are lower in energy than eclipsed ones. In a cyclohexane chair, large groups prefer equatorial positions to avoid 1,3-diaxial strain.

read.title: Chains that twist
text: Alkanes contain only C–C and C–H single bonds, so they are the simplest organic compounds and the base for naming everything else. A name starts from the longest continuous chain (meth-, eth-, prop-, but-, pent-, and so on). Number the chain from the end that reaches a branch first, give each branch a locant, and list the branches in alphabetical order. CH₃CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃ is therefore 2-methylbutane, not 3-methylbutane.

Single bonds rotate, and the different shapes produced are called conformations. Sighting down a C–C bond in a Newman projection shows that ethane is most stable when its hydrogens are staggered. The eclipsed form costs about 12 kJ/mol of torsional strain, small enough that rotation is rapid at room temperature. In butane, the anti conformation, with the two methyl groups opposite each other, is lowest in energy.

Rings add angle strain. Cyclopropane's 60° angles make it highly strained, but cyclohexane avoids nearly all strain by puckering into a chair. Each carbon of the chair has one axial and one equatorial position. Axial groups bump into the other axial hydrogens on the same face, so a large substituent spends most of its time equatorial.
